question_en: An analyst has compiled the following information: Country Z is an open economy, trading at world prices, and does not currently trade with any of the other three countries. Assuming equal consumption of both commodities, which country will benefit the most from a trading relationship with Country Z?
explanation_en: An autarky is a country that produces all goods and services consumed internally and does not trade with others. An autarkic economy is considered a closed economy. Domestic prices within a country are a function of its ability to produce those goods with only domestic resources and are known as the autarkic prices. Countries that do not place restrictions on imports and exports are known as open economies. Open economies are said to practice free trade as they import and export at the world's price for goods and services (eg, Country Z). The further away the world price is relative to a country's autarkic price, the greater the potential trade benefit for the autarky. A country's terms of trade benefit the most if world export prices are greater than its autarkic price and world import prices are less than its autarkic price since the country can achieve greater purchasing power. In this scenario, all the autarkies produce coffee below world price and sugar above world price. Thus, if all three traded with other countries, each would export coffee and import sugar. The net terms-of-trade improvement would be greatest for Country A since it would sell (ie, export) coffee at the world price of $1.10 and buy (ie, import) sugar at the world price of $0.40, netting a $0.50 improvement. (Choices B and C) The net terms-of-trade improvement for Country B is $0.15. For Country C, it is $0.40.

It is a tax on imported goods that is usually paid as a higher price for the goods and usually results in a loss to the net welfare of the economy. Tariffs cause inefficiencies in both the supply and production functions of the economy; these losses are known as deadweight losses. In the diagram above, the supply deadweight loss is Region B and the demand deadweight loss is Region D. Before the tariff, all suppliers had per-unit production costs of €200 or less. The demand deadweight loss is evidenced from the reduced domestic demand after the tariff. question_en: A country that is a price taker in the international market imposes a per-unit tariff of €50 on imported mobile phones. The table below shows domestic consumption, domestic production, and mobile phone prices before and after the tariff's imposition: The total deadweight loss (in €) from the imposition of the tariff is closest to:
explanation_en: Most economists believe greater overall welfare is attained when countries engage in international trade rather than by attempting self-sufficiency in meeting domestic demand (ie, autarky). The gains from international trade derive from each country concentrating on the production of goods it produces relatively more efficiently and trading for goods it produces relatively less efficiently. Gains result from specialization and economies of scale. The gains from trade are not shared equally; there are winners and losers. On one hand, industries expanding to meet export opportunities will benefit from higher prices, due to increased foreign demand, and their employees will benefit from greater job opportunities and higher wages (Choice C). On the other hand, the industries' domestic customers must pay higher prices. In addition, industries facing import competition will suffer domestic market share decline. As such industries contract, they will employ fewer workers. (Choice A) Increased trade results in greater consumer choice. This is due both to imported goods competing with domestic suppliers and the introduction of previously unavailable products.

question_en: Which of the following is most accurate with regard to a dual-class share structure?
option_a: Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of ownership.
option_b: It may grant founders superior voting control even if their ownership level falls below 50%.
option_c: It typically grants outside shareholders greater voting power than insiders and family
explanation_en: Normally, public companies have a share structure that grants each shareholder proportional voting power based on the number of shares held. For example, a shareholder who owns 50% of the company controls 50% of the votes. One exception to the general rule is a dual-class structure, where different share classes allow different numbers of votes per share (eg, Class A at one vote per share vs. Class B at two votes per share). A dual-class structure may create disproportional voting power relative to share ownership. Insiders (eg, founders) commonly hold Class B shares, which grant them dominant voting control on important issues (eg, board elections or strategic decisions) even if their share ownership falls below 50%. (Choice A) Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of share ownership only if all shares grant the same number of votes. Different share classes allow for different votes per share in a dual-class structure. (Choice C) Class B shares are granted mainly to insiders and family members and not to outside shareholders; therefore, greater voting power is typically held by insiders and family members.

question_en: A company's analyst made the following after-tax cash flow projections for two independent investments: The cost of capital is the company's hurdle rate of 12.5%. Based on the internal rate of return (IRR) approach, which of the following actions is most appropriate for the company?
option_c: Invest in both Projects A and B.
explanation_en: Companies often make choices among possible projects since there are constraints that prevent them from pursuing all net present value (NPV) positive projects. Depending on the circumstances, these project interactions include: project sequencing, capital rationing, or mutually exclusive projects. With project sequencing, projects are lined up sequentially through time, so that investing in Project X creates the option to invest in Project Y. The decision to invest in Project Y (or other future projects) will be based on the completion and success of Project X. For example, a company may begin delivery services in a new region. Depending on the success of the delivery service, the company will decide whether to build a distribution center in that region. (Choice A) Capital rationing is the process of allocating limited resources (at any one time) to the most profitable combination of projects. This occurs when a company has more positive NPV projects than its resources will allow it to pursue. (Choice B) Mutually exclusive projects are those that compete directly with each other, so only one project can be selected. This is usually due to a resource constraint.

of return (r) as the discount rate. As a result, projects with a positive NPV add to company value.

are estimated at the beginning of the asset's life (Choice C). Therefore, the only variable that can change the depreciation expense will be the
actual number of units produced. Using the units-of-production method, if the depreciation expense increases each year, the number of units
produced is also expected to grow.

scenario, although production and COGS are expected to grow, that does not suggest the net margin will increase.

upper and lower limit.
The upper limit is the net realizable value (NRV), which is the selling price net of the costs to complete and sell the inventory. In this
scenario, NRV = Selling price − Selling cost − Completion cost, so NRV = 140 − 10 − 30 = 100.
The lower limit is the NRV minus a normal profit margin. In this scenario, the lower limit is NRV − Normal profit margin = 100 − 7 = 93.
MV is always the middle number of the replacement cost (RC), upper limit, and lower limit when ranked in order:
If RC > Upper > Lower, MV is the upper limit.
If Upper > RC > Lower, MV is the RC.
If Upper > Lower > RC, MV is the lower limit.
In this case, the MV is the RC of $96 per unit since it is within the upper and lower limits and is lower than the historical cost of the inventory.
(Choice B) $100 is the upper limit for MV, which is capped at the upper limit only when RC exceeds the upper limit.
(Choice C) $105 is the company's historical cost. The inventory's NRV is lower than its historical cost, so the NRV should be reported.

question_en: A company that reports under IFRS is valuing its year-end inventory. It has collected the following information (in CHF millions): Based on this data, the inventory value (in CHF millions) reported on its balance sheet is closest to:
explanation_en:
Inventory is initially recorded on a company's balance sheet at historic cost. However, companies are required to regularly reassess this value. If
the inventory's value falls below its cost (eg, spoils, becomes obsolete, declines in selling price), the company must write down the inventory to
reflect the new, lower value, which becomes the carrying value.
IFRS require companies to report the carrying value of inventory at the lower of cost or net realizable value (NRV). The NRV is the estimated
selling price less the cost of completing and selling the inventory.
In this scenario, the NRV of the inventory is CHF 180 million (240 − 60). This is higher than the cost of 175, so no write down is taken and the
inventory remains at 175.
(Choice A) 165 is the replacement value, which is not used by IFRS in valuing inventory. The replacement value is used by companies reporting
under US GAAP and using LIFO or retail inventory methods when valuing inventory.
(Choice C) 180 is the NRV, which is greater than the historical cost. Since inventory is required to be valued at the lower of cost and NRV, the
company would not be permitted to increase the value of its inventory above 175.

If the market price is less than the exercise price, then the put buyer has the right to sell the underlying asset at a higher price than the existing market price. The difference between the exercise price and the market price is the put buyer's payoff. If the market price is not lower than the exercise price, then the put buyer will not exercise the option, and there is no payoff. Therefore, the put buyer's payoff is the greater of (exercise price – market price) and zero. In this scenario, the put's exercise price at expiration is GBP 76, and the value of the underlying is GBP 83. The payoff is the greater of (76 – 83) = GBP −7 and zero, so the payoff is GBP 0. Due to an impairment charge, the carrying value of the machine is closest to:
explanation_en:
Impairment charges are recognized when an asset's carrying amount, measured as historical cost minus accumulated depreciation, is greater
than its recoverable value. US GAAP defines the recoverable amount as simply the undiscounted expected future cash flows. In this case,
the carrying amount ($31,000) exceeds the recoverable amount ($28,000).
The impaired asset is written down to a new carrying value with a new depreciation schedule. Under US GAAP, the asset would be written down
to fair value (ie, value if sold [$22,000]). This fair value estimate becomes the new carrying amount.
In contrast, IFRS defines the recoverable amount and the new carrying value as the greater of the asset's fair value less costs to sell the asset
($22,000 − $2,500) or the discounted future cash flows ($26,500) that the asset is expected to generate (Choices A and C).

explanation_en: An owner of an asset is exposed to the risk that the commodity price will fall between now and when it is sold. Selling an asset forward means that the seller commits to deliver that asset at a future date for a guaranteed price. Selling forward eliminates the seller's price risk, but it also means that the seller does not benefit if the asset's spot price is higher than the contracted price when the contract expires. Although the price the farmer receives at expiration is guaranteed, the relative value of the contract varies prior to expiration depending on how spot prices of the underlying asset change. At expiration, the value of the contract is the difference between the spot price and the forward price. Prior to that time, the contract's value is the difference between the asset's current spot price and the present value of the forward price. Any gain to one party from a change in the forward contract's value is exactly offset by the other party's loss. In this example, any increase in spot wheat prices prior to expiration causes the contract's value to increase to the long party. As the farmer is short, an increase in the contract's value represents a loss. (Choice B) The price that the farmer receives at the contract's expiration does not change, but the value of the contract changes as the underlying asset's price changes. (Choice C) The value of any contract to the short party increases only if the price of the underlying asset decreases.

question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two 18-month forward contracts, each for a different underlying asset: If the risk-free rate is 2.8%, the forward price of Asset Y is most likely:

explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in Arbitrage-free derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and Replication risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives Risk-neutral and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Derivative pricing is based on three key concepts: Arbitrage-free pricing assumes market prices are free of arbitrage opportunities. Derivative pricing is risk-neutral since arbitrage-free markets guarantee risk-free positions that earn the risk-free rate. Equivalent positions can be created through replication using combinations of the underlying asset, a risk-free asset, and a derivative. Derivative prices must reflect the risk-free rate since riskless positions can be created by combining an underlying asset (eg, long a bond) with related derivatives (eg, short bond futures). Similarly, derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying asset with the risk-free asset. Replicated positions that are economically equivalent should trade at economically equivalent prices. Thus, the price of a derivative reflects the value of a replication strategy. If an economically equivalent condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that riskless profits can no longer be earned and arbitrage-free pricing is achieved. This arbitrage-free pricing renders investors risk-neutral, meaning that the risk premiums required by investors to hold the underlying asset have no effect on derivative pricing (Choice B). (Choice C) The price of a derivative contract is dependent on the price of the underlying asset and the terms of the contract, such as the strike price and exercise date. This does not imply that the underlying asset's expected rate of return will be the same as the derivative's expected rate of return.

Derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying with the risk-free asset. Economically equivalent positions should
trade at prices that result in equal returns. If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer
be earned. Arbitrage-free pricing means that investor risk aversion has no impact on derivative pricing. Therefore, derivative pricing is described
as risk-neutral pricing.
By combining positions in the underlying asset (eg, long bond) and the derivative (eg, short bond futures), investors can create riskless
positions. Since riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return, the expected payoffs are discounted at the risk-free rate when pricing

(Choice A) An absence of arbitrage profits means derivatives are fairly priced relative to the underlying asset. In that case, taking offsetting
positions in the derivative and an appropriate replication strategy earns the risk-free rate of return, resulting in the risk-free rate (not zero) being
the appropriate discount rate.
(Choice C) An asset's required rate of return is appropriate for valuing assets but not for pricing derivatives. Derivative prices are derived from

explanation_en: Ratio analysis limitations Heterogeneous operations Inconsistent results Ratios alone are incomplete Accounting differences Analysts often using ratio analysis to assess a company's financial performance or position. Although ratio analysis may provide useful insight, it also comes with limitations: Heterogeneity in operation: If the company's divisions individually operate in distinct industries, then combining performance may oversimplify data at an aggregate level and not provide insight into divisional performance. | Revenue | 3.4 | 3.7 |
| Current assets | 5.0 | 5.2 |
| Current liabilities | 4.0 | 4.4 |

Based on this data, working capital turnover for 20X6 is closest to:
explanation_en: Activity ratios measure how efficiently a company utilizes its assets. The numerator is commonly an income statement item (eg revenue, COGS); the denominator is commonly a balance sheet item (eg, inventory, accounts payable). Working capital (WC) turnover measures how efficiently a company generates sales (revenue) from its current working capital. Working capital is defined as current assets (eg, accounts receivable, inventory) less current liabilities (eg, accounts payable). A high WC turnover suggests that the company is more efficient at using its short-term assets and liabilities to support sales. In this question, divide 20X6 revenue by the average working capital values to calculate working capital turnover: WC turnover(20X6) = Revenue(20X6) / [(WC(20X5) + WC(20X6)) divided by 2] = 3.7 / [(1.0 + 0.8) divided by 2] = 4.11. It is important to note that income statement items (ie, revenue) reflect what happens throughout a period, whereas balance sheet items (inventory) reflect the balance at the end of the period. Therefore, in most ratios that mix income statement with balance sheet items, the balance sheet item is averaged to better capture asset levels throughout the period. (Choice A) 3.94 results from incorrectly averaging both years' revenue in the numerator. (Choice C) 4.63 results from including only 20X6's working capital in the denominator.

explanation_en:
Return on common equity (ROCE) gauges the amount of residual net income (after accounting for preferred dividends) generated relative to
common equity. Preferred dividends are subtracted from net income since common shareholders receive distributions only after preferred

calculated as net income / average total equity.

assets), has worsened. Both ratios are trending down over time, indicating that the company has become less efficient at using its assets to
generate sales.
(Choice C) The stock price has become less expensive over time relative to company fundamentals, as indicated by the decreasing price-to-book
(P/B) and price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios here. This suggests that the investors pay less for the stock relative to the company's earnings and book
value.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.11 Financial Analysis Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en: An analyst gathers the following data to compare two companies' performance. The analyst calculates only three ratios: Debt-to-EBITDA, net profit margin, and total asset turnover. Based only on these three ratios, the analyst can most appropriately conclude that Company A has better:
explanation_en:
Analysts use integrated financial ratio analysis to gauge a company's performance in terms of its activity or efficiency, liquidity, solvency, and
profitability.
Activity ratios measure how efficiently a company utilizes its assets.
Liquidity ratios measure how well a company can cover its short-term obligations with cash or with assets that are easily converted to cash.
Solvency ratios measure a company's ability to satisfy its long-term obligations.
Profitability ratios measure a company's return on sales and return on investments. Return on sales measures the margin earned from
sales. Return on investment measures the profit from invested capital (eg, equity).
From the information provided in the question, solvency is measured by Debt-to-EBITDA ratio, efficiency is measured by total asset turnover,
and profitability is measured by net profit margin. After calculating the three ratios, the analyst can most appropriately conclude that Company
A has better efficiency (0.83 vs. 0.50) since it is better at utilizing its assets to generate sales.
(Choice A) Company B has better solvency as measured by a lower Debt-to-EBITDA ratio.
(Choice C) Company B has better profitability as measured by net profit margin.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.11 Financial Analysis Techniques - Answers.pdf
question_en:
A company reports the following information:

| (MXN millions) | 20X4 | 20X3 |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 15,000 | 13,500 |
| Cost of goods sold | 5,000 | 4,000 |
| Operating expenses | 2,500 | 2,300 |
| Interest | 200 | 1,100 |
| Taxes | 800 | 1,200 |
| Dividends paid | 1,500 | 100 |

Based only on this information, which of the following best describes the change in the company's profitability?
option_a: Operating profit margin and net profit margin both increased.
option_b: Operating profit margin and net profit margin both decreased.
option_c: Operating profit margin decreased and net profit margin increased.
explanation_en:
A company's profit margin, a type of profitability ratio, measures a company's profit relative to its revenue. Different types of profit margins incorporate different expenses to determine a company's profitability.
Here, find the changes in operating profit margin and net profit margin to determine how the company's profitability changed:
- Determine the operating profit margin by calculating operating income and comparing it to revenue. Operating income is earnings that remain after subtracting COGS and operating expenses from revenue.
- Determine the net profit margin by calculating net income and comparing it to revenue. To calculate net income, subtract all expenses (ie, including interest and taxes) from revenue.
The operating profit margin declined from 53.33% to 50.00%. The net profit margin increased from 36.30% to 43.33%.

question_en:
A consultant gathers the following profitability ratios for a company:

| Profitability Ratio (%) | 20X1 | 20X2 | 20X3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gross profit margin | 31.00 | 31.70 | 32.10 |
| Operating profit margin | 10.10 | 10.00 | 8.90 |
| Pretax margin | 9.90 | 9.90 | 6.90 |

Based on this information, over this period the company most likely improved its ability to cover:
explanation_en:
Profit margins (profit / revenue) indicate a company's ability to generate adequate sales to cover various costs:
Gross margin measures ability to cover COGS, which are costs directly attributable to producing the goods and services sold (eg, raw
material costs, production wages, distribution costs).
Operating margin measures ability to further cover operating expenses such as marketing or research and development.
Pretax margin measures ability to further cover certain nonoperating expenses such as financing costs (eg, interest).
Net margin measures ability to further cover taxes.
In this scenario, gross margin increased over time, which means the company improved its ability to cover COGS, including raw material costs.
(Choice B) Operating margin decreased over time, which suggests a worsened ability to cover operating expenses.
(Choice C) Pretax margin remained unchanged, which suggests deterioration or no improvement in the company's ability to cover nonoperating
expenses (before taxes).

question_en:
An analyst collects the following annual data for a company:

| | Company | Industry Average |
|---|---|---|
| Days of sales outstanding | 45.10 | 30.09 |
| Total asset turnover | 1.20 | 1.15 |
| Days of inventory on hand | 25.42 | 29.77 |

Which of the following best describes how the company's efficiency compares with the industry?
option_a: The company has a receivable turnover that is better.
option_b: The company has more effective inventory management.
option_c: The company produces less revenue for a given asset level.
explanation_en:
Activity ratios measure how efficient a company is and indicate its operational performance. Days of inventory on hand (DOH), an activity ratio,
indicates management's effectiveness in overseeing its inventory. DOH is the average number of days it takes a company to convert inventory
(eg, current assets) into revenue.
The ratio is calculated as the number of days in the period divided by the company's inventory turnover (COGS/average inventory). Lower DOH
suggests that management has a lower drain on company assets and generates revenue more quickly. Here, it has more effective inventory
management than its peers since its DOH is less than the industry average (25.42 < 29.77).
(Choice A) Using the days of sales outstanding formula, the company's receivable turnover of 8.09 (45.10 = 365 / receivable turnover) is lower
than the industry's of 12.13 (30.09 = 365/receivable turnover). Its receivable turnover is worse, not better than the industry average. If the days of
sales outstanding (DSO) is lower than the industry average, so is the receivable turnover since they are effectively the same; DSO converts
turnover into a time measurement.
(Choice C) Total asset turnover is a ratio that measures a company's overall efficiency; a higher ratio means the company is more efficient at
generating revenue for a given level of assets. The company produces more revenue for a given asset level than its peers since its total asset
turnover is greater (1.20 > 1.15) than the industry average.

question_en:
An analyst completes the following DuPont analysis on two companies:

|  | Company X | Company Y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tax burden | 0.75 | 0.75 |
| Interest burden | 0.80 | 0.80 |
| EBIT margin | 0.10 | 0.18 |
| Asset turnover | 0.90 | 1.20 |
| Leverage | 3.00 | 1.20 |

Compared with Company Y, Company X mostly likely has a:
option_a: lower ROE and is more efficient.
option_b: higher ROE and has a higher profit margin.
option_c: higher ROE and a higher proportion of debt.
explanation_en:
DuPont analysis entails decomposing ROE into five components. In this case, multiply the five components together to find the ROE of
Companies X and Y, which are 16.20% and 15.55%, respectively. Company X has a higher ROE despite its lower profitability (0.10 vs. 0.18) and
efficiency (0.90 vs. 1.20) compared with Company Y's. Company X has greater leverage (ie, proportion of debt) than Company Y (3.00 vs 1.20),
which is why Company X's ROE is greater than Company Y's (Choices A and B).
Leverage is a gauge of solvency as measured by the company's assets relative to its average total equity. The higher the ratio, the more the
company finances its assets with debt.

question_en:
A company uses LIFO to determine the valuation for inventory and reports the following under US GAAP:

| Selected Items from Financial Statements | 20X7 | 20X6 |
|---|---|---|
| Current assets (USD millions) | 1,400 | 1,660 |
| Current liabilities (USD millions) | 333 | 400 |

The company discloses that its LIFO reserve in 20X7 was $277 and in 20X6 was $450. If the company used FIFO instead of LIFO for its inventory valuation, then over the last year, the company's current ratio most likely:
explanation_en: FIFO inventory = Inventory valued under LIFO + LIFO reserve. Companies that use LIFO (last-in, first-out) to value inventory often report lower inventory and higher expense than companies that use FIFO (first-in, first-out). Under US GAAP, companies that use LIFO must report the difference between inventory under LIFO and FIFO as the LIFO reserve. When preparing comparisons between companies that differ in their use of LIFO and FIFO inventory valuation, add back the LIFO reserve to convert LIFO inventory to FIFO. In this case, to find the company's current ratio as it would be under the FIFO method, add the LIFO reserve to current assets (inventory is a part of current assets). Adjusted current assets: 20X7: 1,400 + 277 = 1,677; 20X6: 1,680 + 450 = 2,130. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Using current assets adjusted for FIFO, the current ratio decreases year over year from 5.33 to 5.04: 20X7: 1,677 / 333 = 5.04; 20X6: 2,130 / 400 = 5.33. (Choice B) The current ratio would have remained the same with no adjustment for differences in the accounting method. (Choice C) The current ratio would have increased by subtracting the LIFO reserve from current assets. To adjust for differences between LIFO and FIFO, add the LIFO reserves to inventory. This increases current assets. Things to remember: When comparing companies, some of which use LIFO and some of which use FIFO for inventory reporting, make their inventory values comparable by adding the LIFO reserve to the LIFO inventory valuation.

question_en: A hedge fund will commit $15 million to a short sale of an exchange-listed stock. The fund sells short the maximum number of shares allowable when the margin requirement is 0.4. The relevant information is shown in the table below: No interest is paid for the borrowed shares, but there is a short rebate on the sales proceeds. If the fund closes out the position in exactly 1 year, the total percentage return is closest to:

A short sale is profitable if the repurchase price is lower than the sales price ("buy low, sell high" = "sell high, buy low"). The profit depends largely on the number of shares that are shorted. Borrowing shares represents leverage, so all short sales are margin transactions. The maximum number of shares that can be sold short is a function of the short seller's equity in the transaction. In addition to the difference between the sales and repurchase prices, the return on a short sale also depends on: the short rebate: interest earned by the short seller on the short sales proceeds and calculated as a function of the investment value and the broker’s deposit rate. dividends that are paid on the shares until they are repurchased, which the short seller must pay the lender. commissions and other trading costs subtracted from the proceeds (not a factor in this question). question_en: In an order-driven market system, the following buy limit orders for a stock are listed in the system's limit book: Each order is listed for 200 shares. Based on the commonly used order precedence hierarchy, if the current market price is $15.10 and the exchange receives a market sell order for 500 shares, then the orders most likely to be fully executed are:
explanation_en:
Order-driven system: priority rules for filling limit orders
The most aggressively priced orders (eg, highest-priced
Highest priority:
buys, lowest-priced sells) filled first
Price
Price takes priority over time and visibility
Orders of fully visible size have priority over those of partially
Next priority:
or fully hidden size
Visibility
Visibility takes priority over time
Next priority: Same-price orders filled based on time of receipt
Time received Earliest received = Higher priority
An order-driven system is used by nearly every stock exchange, with rules that match the buyers' and sellers' orders. Three basic rules
determine how limit orders are executed ("filled").
The first rule is based on price. Orders with the most aggressive prices (eg, highest buy price, lowest sell price) receive the highest priority. If
more than one order has the same price, priority is given to orders that are fully visible, meaning that the entire number of shares covered by the
order is known. Orders in which the size is hidden, either fully or partially (ie, iceberg orders, have lower priority than fully visible orders.
For orders with the same price and visibility, priority is based on when each order was received. The earliest-received order has the highest
priority, followed by the second earliest, etc.
In this case, Order 3 has the highest price, so it will be filled first even though it arrived last at the exchange. Orders 1 and 2 have the same price.
Order 1 arrived first, but since it is an iceberg order, it drops behind Order 2 in priority. Order 1 receives only 100 shares; Orders 2 and 3 are filled
entirely (Choices A and C).

question_en:
A limit order book contains the following information for a stock:

| Bid Size | Price | Ask Size |
|---|---|---|
| 6,000 | 15.20 |  |
| 10,000 | 15.22 |  |
| 8,000 | 15.25 |  |
|  | 15.27 | 6,000 |
|  | 15.30 | 10,000 |
|  | 15.33 | 12,000 |

The market bid-ask quote is most likely:
explanation_en:
Market makers (eg, dealers) provide liquidity in the marketplace by transacting with other buyers and sellers. Dealers are willing to buy at bid
prices and sell at ask prices (offer prices) and profit from the difference (ie, bid-ask spread). The market bid-ask quote is the highest bid price
(best bid) and lowest ask price (best ask).
In this instance, the highest bid is 15.25, and the lowest ask is 15.27. This means that 15.25 is the best (highest) price that a seller can sell to a
dealer who is willing to buy, and 15.27 is the best (lowest) price that a buyer can buy from a dealer who is willing to sell.

question_en: A market's limit order book for a stock is listed below: A buy limit order for 200 shares makes a new market when it is priced at:
explanation_en:
The prices at which market participants are willing to buy (sell) are called bid (offer) prices. When a new limit order is entered that is at current
market prices, the order is said to:
Make the market if it matches the current best bid (buy) or offer (sell) price and is added to the order book, as is the case in this scenario.
Take the market if it is immediately executed, since the order takes what the market is currently quoting. A buyer takes the lowest (best)
offer and a seller takes the highest (best) bid (Choice C).
When a new market order is entered that is between the current highest bid and lowest offer, it is said to make a new market (Choice B).

question_en: A leveraged security position is held with only the minimum required equity. If the minimum equity requirement is reduced, the most likely consequence is that the position's risk is:
option_a: increased since the securities are less valuable collateral for the margin loan.
option_b: decreased since the maximum possible loss is reduced by having less equity in the position.
option_c: increased since any security price changes will be a larger percentage of the position's
explanation_en:
In a leveraged position, a trader invests less equity than the security's market value (ie, buys on margin) and borrows the balance. For any
position, leveraged or unleveraged, gains or losses are the change in the position's value. For a leveraged position the equity is less than 100% of
the position's value, therefore any percentage change the position's value will produce a greater percentage change in the equity.
Leveraged long positions exhibit a wider dispersion of returns than unleveraged long positions since the percentage gains (losses) are greater
when prices rise (fall). Therefore, leveraged long positions are riskier. The difference in risk is related directly to the leverage ratio: if a position's
equity is reduced in line with a reduction in the minimum margin requirement, risk increases since the leverage has increased.
(Choice A) The collateral value of securities is based on market value and is not affected by the margin requirement.
(Choice B) Losses are not limited to the trader's equity in the position. Holders of leveraged security positions incur losses equal to the full
amount of any loss on the entire position.

question_en: With respect to cumulative preference shares, dividends that were not paid in prior periods are most likely:
option_a: forfeited and not paid to cumulative preference shareholders in the future.
option_b: accrued and paid to cumulative preference shareholders in the future before paying common shareholders.
option_c: accrued and paid to cumulative preference shareholders in the future only after paying
explanation_en:
Types of preference shares (preferred stock)
Cumulative Accrues for past dividends that are unpaid
Noncumulative Does not accrue dividends that are undeclared and unpaid in past periods
Participating Allows for additional dividend payments if company profits exceed a certain threshold
Nonparticipating Fixed dividend; no additional payments based on company performance
Convertible Can convert into a specified number of common shares
Callable Allows issuer to buy back shares from investors for a specified price
Putable Allows investors to sell shares back to issuer for a specified price
Preferred (preference) shares ownership represents a form of equity investment in a company. Preference shares may grant certain benefits to
preferred shareholders such as high dividend payments and in some cases conversion rights (to common stock). Furthermore, dividend
payments to preferred shareholders take precedence over dividend payments to common shareholders. Preferred dividends can be cumulative
or noncumulative.
For cumulative preference dividends, if a company does not pay a dividend (or dividends) in one period (or several periods), the unpaid dividend
accrues and is owed in the future. Conversely, for noncumulative preference dividends, the company does not accrue (and does not owe payment
for) unpaid dividends from past periods.
(Choice A) Unpaid dividends on cumulative preferred shares are accrued and owed to preferred shareholders.
(Choice C) Payments of past unpaid dividends are due to preference shareholders before any dividends can be distributed to common
shareholders.

question_en:
An analyst observes the following market data for one American put option:

| Selected Data (in CAD) |  |
| --- | --- |
| Stock price | 48 |
| Strike price | 50 |
| Option premium | 4 |

This option's moneyness is best described as:
explanation_en: Moneyness refers to the relationship between an option's strike price and the underlying stock price and is indicative of the option's intrinsic value. An option trading at the money or out of the money has no intrinsic value. An option trading in the money has intrinsic value: For an in-the-money call option, the underlying stock price is greater than the strike price. This gives the call owner the right to buy the stock at a price lower than the market price, which in turn gives the option intrinsic value. For an in-the-money put option, the strike price is greater than the underlying stock price. This gives the put owner the right to sell the stock at a price higher than the market price, which in turn gives the option intrinsic value. In this scenario, the put option's underlying stock price is less than its strike price. Therefore, the option is trading in the money. Note that the option's premium is irrelevant to determining the option's intrinsic value; it would, however, be relevant to determining the option's profit at exercise. (Choice B) If the stock price equals the strike price, the option is trading at the money (ATM). At expiration, an ATM option is economically equivalent to owning the underlying asset. (Choice C) For a call option, if the stock price is less than the strike price, the option is trading out of the money (OTM) and has no intrinsic value. The same is true for a put option if the stock price is greater than the strike price.

question_en: A contingency provision contained in the indenture of a bond issued by a corporation most likely refers to:
option_a: the issuer's ability to defer coupon payments if certain conditions are met.
option_b: the bondholder's ability to force the corporation to redeem the bond before maturity.
option_c: the issuer's right to incur additional debt while some or all of the original amount is still
explanation_en: Typical bond contingency provisions Callability Issuer has right to redeem bond before maturity Putability Bondholder can require issuer to redeem bond before maturity Bondholder can convert bond into a predetermined number of issuer's Convertibility common shares Contingency provisions in the context of bonds are very specific and refer to the rights of the issuer and/or bondholders with respect to how a bond can be redeemed or disposed of. The most common types of contingency provisions concern whether a bond can be called, put, or converted. A putable bond gives its holder the right to require that the issuer redeem the bond before maturity. The redemption price is established in the indenture, in addition to any other relevant provisions such as when the bondholder must act. This right (ie, the put) can be valuable to the bondholder, and that value allows the issuer to pay a lower coupon rate. (Choice A) The issuer's right to defer coupon payments does not relate to redeeming or converting the bond, so it is not properly categorized as a contingency. (Choice C) Provisions concerning an issuer's ability to incur additional debt are a covenant, or promise, of actions that the issuer agrees to take (ie, affirmative covenants) or not take (ie, negative covenants).

question_en: The repo margin most accurately describes:
option_a: the rate of return earned by the repo lender.
option_b: the difference between the market value of the collateral and the amount loaned.
option_c: the amount of additional collateral required by the repo lender in addition to the repo
explanation_en: A repurchase agreement (ie, repo) is a type of short-term debt. It is structured as the sale of an asset, typically a high-quality, short-term bond that the seller agrees to repurchase at a future date for a specified amount. Since the terms of the agreement are known in advance, a repo can be viewed as a short-term secured loan. The repo seller is the borrower and the repo buyer is the lender. The lender is exposed to the risk that the borrower will be unable to repurchase the asset when the agreement matures. Although the buyer can sell the collateral if the seller defaults, it is possible that its market value will have declined from when the repo was initiated. To mitigate this risk, the amount loaned is less than the value of the collateral. The difference is the repo margin. In the example above, the repo margin is $1,010 − 1,000 = $10. (Choice A) The repo rate is the lender's return from the transaction (ie, the repurchase agreement's interest rate). In the example above, the price ($2 higher) that the seller pays to repurchase the asset is equivalent to the interest on the original $1,000 loan. In this case the repo rate is 0.2% for the two-month period, or 1.2% annually. (Choice C) The financial instrument that the buyer purchases is the only collateral in a repo. The repo margin is a form of credit enhancement for the loan, but it is not additional collateral.

question_en: An analyst has compiled the following data on a corporate bond: The price impact from an instantaneous 80 basis points of spread narrowing is closest to (%):
explanation_en: The price change of a bond is a function of its modified duration, its convexity, and a change in its yield. The yield of a corporate bond is a function of interest rates and the bond's yield spread. The yield spread is the difference in yields between the corporate bond and a government issue of the same maturity, reflecting the greater credit and liquidity risks (ie, spread risk) of the corporate bond. A change in spread can significantly impact the price of a bond. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. Therefore, narrowing spreads (ie, smaller spreads) positively impact prices and widening spreads (ie, larger spreads) have a negative impact. Note that the negative sign in the price impact equation accounts for this inverse relationship. Price impact can be determined by entering the values into the formula: (Choice A) 6.86% is the estimated price decline if the spread widens by 80 basis points. (Choice B) 7.15% results from approximating price impact (L54761) using only modified duration, which is appropriate for only small changes in spreads.

explanation_en: Issuers create mortgage pass-through securities (ie, pass-throughs) by pooling individual mortgage loans and using the pool as collateral for the pass-through security, which is then sold to investors. Investors receive cash returns generated from the pool of monthly mortgage payments. The mortgage pool usually consists of multiple mortgages with different interest rates. The pass-through rate (ie, coupon rate that pass-through investors receive) equals the weighted average coupon (WAC) less servicing and administrative fees. The WAC is the weighted average of the mortgage rates for the pooled mortgages, with the weights being each mortgage balance as a percentage of the total balances. In this scenario, the WAC is 4.75% and the fees are 0.25%, so the pass-through rate is 4.50%. (Choice A) 4.48% results from taking the simple average, not the weighted average, of the coupons. (Choice C) 4.75% results from not subtracting the servicing fee from the WAC.

explanation_en: Futures price = Spot price + Cost of holding underlying − Benefits of holding underlying Derivative pricing is based on the no-arbitrage principle (ie, arbitrage-free pricing). This means that economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns. If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned. Futures price − Spot price = Cost of holding underlying − Benefits of holding underlying Benefits < costs Futures > spot Benefits > costs Futures < spot Benefits = costs Futures = spot Taking a long position in futures avoids the costs and forgoes any benefits of holding the underlying asset. For equivalent positions (eg, long stock = long stock futures + long a risk-free bond) to earn equal returns, futures and spot prices must differ by the net cost of holding the underlying asset until the expiration of the futures contract. When the benefits of holding the asset are greater than the costs of holding it, there is added value in holding the asset, so futures prices are below the spot price and not equal to or above it (Choices B and C). The net cost of holding a position in the underlying asset or commodity is called the cost of carry. The carry, as it is sometimes called, reflects the net of: costs—charges for storage, insurance, or financing the underlying position, versus benefits—income (ie, dividends or interest) or convenience yield from holding the underlying.

question_en: The seed investor of a three-year-old hedge fund that invests in high-yield private placements requests a redemption of £20 million. Fund details are listed below: Which of the following is the most likely outcome?

explanation_en: Some types of alternative investments (ie, private equity or real estate) have variable cash flows in which investors often experience low or negative cash flows early in the investment, with cash flows eventually turning positive. Ideally, measuring returns capture both the amount and the timing of cash flows. IRR is the primary measure used to assess investments with variable cash flows. The IRR calculation considers the timing of an investment's cash flows and its overall time frame, as well as the opportunity cost of the capital committed to an investment. The multiple of invested capital (MOIC) (ie, money multiple) is a ratio of total value of all residual asset values and distributions to the initial investment; thus, it is expressed as a multiple of the initial investment. This is viewed as a shortcut method that does not consider the investment time frame. IRR's main advantage over MOIC is that it accounts for how cash flow timing affects returns. IRR also has two key disadvantages: It is less intuitive than MOIC: MOIC illustrates how much an investor has received relative to the amount initially invested (Choice A). IRR is more complicated to calculate: MOIC is simply a multiple at a point in time and ignores effects from the timing of cash flows; IRR relies on assumptions about financing and reinvestment rates (Choice B).

explanation_en: Proper asset valuations are necessary for calculating investment performance. Valuation is straightforward when an asset is highly liquid and trades frequently since prices are readily available. Valuation becomes more difficult and subjective when prices cannot be readily observed or when an asset trades infrequently. Internal modeling tends to be used for valuation only if other, more objective methods cannot be applied. Internal modeling is typically used if the asset is: illiquid, not traded on exchanges, not priced by outside sources, or affected by unobservable inputs or assumptions Distressed debt generally fits all these criteria, so hedge funds specializing in distressed debt would likely use internal models to value their assets. (Choice A) Macro hedge funds invest opportunistically across a wide variety of asset classes, including derivatives. The value of certain derivatives such as interest rate swaps or currency swaps depends on rates that are directly observable in the market. (Choice C) Assets that trade regularly on public exchanges have reliable and easily available prices. Hedge funds specializing in fundamental value strategies establish long and short positions on assets that are openly traded in the market, and thus are unlikely to rely on internal models.

Hedge fund fees are often negotiated, enticing investors to commit capital, particularly for new or small hedge funds. These custom fee arrangements can take many forms, but a common arrangement includes founders' shares, which entitle early investors to: permanently lower fees, up to a certain monetary threshold (eg, $100 million invested), or fees that do not apply until the fund grows to a certain size (eg, greater than $100 million AUM). (Choice C) An "either/or" fee structure is not a characteristic of founders' shares and refers to an arrangement of paying either management or incentive fees. For example, an investor may agree to pay a 30% incentive fee if certain performance thresholds are met, but in exchange will not pay an annual management fee.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information requires Members and Candidates to abstain from investment actions if they have material nonpublic information (MNI). Trading on or acting on MNI erodes the public's trust in the fairness of the capital markets. MNI can come from many sources, and a Member or Candidate must evaluate information to decide whether it is MNI before acting on it. Selective disclosure (eg, analysts on a conference call, corporate insiders) does not necessarily make information public. In this question, Ching Liu and ES intentionally disclosed information and gave the analysts the timeline of when that information would be publicly disseminated. This type of selective disclosure is not a violation of the Standard (Choices A and B). However, by agreeing to be part of the select group receiving the information, Bo Wang has a duty to keep this information confidential until it is released publicly by the company. Even though Wang did not directly disclose the MNI, he violated the Standard by using his knowledge of MNI to influence others to act based on this information. Acting on MNI is not limited strictly to that company's securities (eg, ES), any trading based on MNI is a violation of the Standard.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence." Examples include acts that involve lying, cheating, theft, fraud, or other dishonest behavior. However, violations of Standard I(D) are not limited to actions specifically prohibited by the Standard. explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II Integrity of Capital Markets discusses the member's and candidate's responsibility to protect the integrity of the capital markets. Standard II(A) focuses specifically on the use of material nonpublic information. Trading with material nonpublic information ("insider trading") threatens market integrity, which relies on all market participants having fair access to information and no participant having the advantage of using information that is not widely available. The table below is a quick reference for determining whether Standard II(A) is violated: When a firm has material nonpublic information about a stock, it must try to ensure that trading does not violate the Standard. A ban on all trading in the stock is not always necessary or advisable. For example, if a firm acts as a market maker or dealer for a certain security, suspension of market making may signal that the firm has material nonpublic information and, in effect, expose that information. Market-making activities may continue but should be restricted to taking passive, counterparty positions in unsolicited trades. (Choice A) Risk-arbitrage activity (proprietary trading, as when a firm establishes positions for its own profit) should be suspended since there is great potential for illegal gains. (Choice C) The stock should be placed on a "restricted" or "watch" list, and employees should not trade the stock for their personal accounts. Personal trades should be reported periodically and monitored for insider trading activity.

Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts defines a conflict as a matter that reasonably could be expected to "impair [members' or candidates'] independence or objectivity or interfere with their respective duties…." Beck's spouse serves as a director of a company that Beck will be covering as an analyst. This must be disclosed since it potentially interferes with Beck's objectivity. It is irrelevant that Beck wrote reports on the company for his previous employer since he cannot assume the new employer is aware of the relevant facts. The Standard includes all conflicts, not just financial conflicts. Beck's soccer trusteeship is a potential conflict since Beck will have to devote significant time to the association in the coming months. This could interfere with his duties to his employer as well as to his clients. The Standard does not require an actual conflict to exist to trigger disclosure, only that one could "reasonably be expected" to occur (Choice A). (Choice C) Both Beck's spouse serving as a trustee of a company that Beck will be covering as an analyst and his soccer trusteeship pose actual or potential conflicts of interest, which Standard VI(A) requires him to disclose to his new employer.

question_en: Ajay Patel, CFA, is a financial adviser for Eclipse Financial. At a party, Patel discusses financial advisory services with Nira Jain. Jain asks Patel to be her adviser, but Patel states that he cannot accept new clients. Patel recommends Eclipse and states that he has faith in all the company's advisers. Jain agrees to become a client of Eclipse if Patel agrees to meet with her quarterly over dinner, paid for by Jain, to discuss her portfolio allocation. Which of the following best describes Patel's options under the Code and Standards?
option_b: Patel can accept the offer but then must disclose it immediately to Eclipse in writing
option_c: Patel can accept the offer only after disclosing it in writing to Eclipse and receiving approval
explanation_en:
"Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that
competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's
interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved."
Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires Members and Candidates to obtain written permission when third-party,
additional compensation agreements could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with their employers. Permission must be received from
all parties before the agreement can be accepted. The Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary (eg, gifts, benefits) compensation.
In this scenario, accepting Jain's offer to pay for quarterly dinners to discuss portfolio allocation could be perceived as a conflict of interest since
Patel's actions can be perceived as giving Jain preferential treatment. His advice could be viewed as favoring Jain over his own clients and may
run counter to advice given by Eclipse's other advisers. To comply with the Standard, Patel would be required to obtain written permission from
both Jain and Eclipse before accepting the offer so Eclipse can monitor his actions.
(Choice A) Patel is not required to reject the offer so long as he obtains written permission from all parties involved so his employer can monitor
for conflicts.
(Choice B) Informing Eclipse after accepting the offer is a violation of the Standard. Patel must receive permission before agreeing so Eclipse
can decide if the agreement presents a conflict.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities. Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity focuses on ensuring that Members and Candidates who are investment professionals avoid any actions that compromise their independence and objectivity. explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation requires Members and Candidates to avoid any practices that deceive market participants through the distortion of securities prices or trading volume. Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing misleading information) and transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The Standard is not meant to prevent the use of legitimate strategies that limit a trade's impact on the market when trading large positions or low- liquidity stocks. The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is whether the trading strategy is intended to deceive market participants. If the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard. In this scenario, Annika Goncharov uses a legitimate strategy of breaking up a large position of a low-liquidity stock to limit the impact of the sale on the price. Annika's strategy has not violated the Standard (Choice B). Boris Goncharov intends to distort market prices by making market participants believe there are more buyers of Bright Sky Capital's stock than there are. Since market participants cannot see that Boris is driving both the buying and the selling activity, the trading is deceptive and has violated the Standard (Choice C).

explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires members and candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when investing. It is not uncommon for a member or candidate to transact in the same investments as a client or even alongside the client. This situation does not violate the Standard provided that: the client is not disadvantaged by the trade, the member or candidate does not benefit from the client transactions, and the member or candidate adheres to all applicable regulatory requirements. question_en:
A regulator devised a test to determine if distressed banks will go bankrupt and has estimated the following related probabilities:

| Probability that a bank does not pass the test | 0.6200 |
|---|---|
| Joint probability that a bank goes bankrupt and passes the test | 0.0500 |
| Probability that a bank goes bankrupt given that it does not pass the test | 0.7903 |

The probability that a bank goes bankrupt is closest to:
explanation_en: When a question requires a candidate to calculate the probability that an event occurs based on whether a different event occurs or does not occur, this signals the candidate to use the total probability rule: P(bankrupt) = P(bankrupt AND pass) + P(bankrupt AND not pass) = [P(pass) x P(bankrupt | pass)] + [P(not pass) x P(bankrupt | not pass)]. The question asks for the probability of a bank going bankrupt, an event the occurrence of which is related to whether it passes a test. The probability of not passing the test is 0.62, so the probability of passing the test is 1 - 0.62 = 0.38. The joint probability that a bank goes bankrupt and it passes the test is 0.05; the conditional probability that a bank goes bankrupt given that it does not pass the test is 0.7903. The total probability rule can be illustrated as a tree diagram: the first node shows the two unconditional probabilities of whether a bank passes the test or does not pass; the next nodes show the conditional probabilities of bankruptcy and no bankruptcy, based on whether the bank passes the test or not. The two conditional probabilities containing no bankruptcy are irrelevant since the question asks for the probability that a bank goes bankrupt. The joint probability of bankruptcy and passing the test is given in the question as 0.05. The joint probability that a bank goes bankrupt and does not pass the test is calculated as: P(bankrupt AND not pass) = P(not pass) x P(bankrupt | not pass) = 0.62 x 0.7903 = 0.4899. The total probability that a bank goes bankrupt is the sum of the two joint probabilities involving the bank going bankrupt: 0.05 + 0.4899 = 0.5399, or approximately 0.54.

question_en: .A one-week sample of daily closing net asset values for a fund is randomly selected. The observations for the week were 38, 41, 35, 51, and 45. The mean absolute deviation (MAD) for this sample is closest to:
explanation_en:
Mean absolute deviation (MAD) measures dispersion (ie, variability) of observations around the mean. Dispersion refers to the difference
between an observation and the mean. Higher dispersion means that the observations are more spread out around the mean, which indicates a
greater probability of observations that are significantly higher or lower than the mean. In finance, dispersion indicates risk.
Since the sum of all dispersions around the mean equals 0, MAD instead uses the absolute value of each dispersion. The sum of all the absolute
values is divided by the number of observations, which produces the average dispersion. The calculations are shown below:
(Choice A) Data in a sample will be both above and below the mean, so some dispersions around the mean are negative and others are
positive. The sum of all dispersions equals 0, so the average also equals 0. By using the absolute value of the dispersions, MAD always
generates a number ≥ 0.
(Choice C) 6.0 results from dividing the sum of the absolute values by (n − 1), or 4, instead of 5. The number of observations minus 1 is used
only when calculating the standard deviation of a sample. MAD uses the actual number of observations.

would take for the company to exhaust its quick assets (eg, cash + short-term marketable investments + receivables) when paying for its
ongoing expenses. If its DIR is low, the company may not be able to pay its bills.
Some may understand this ratio as a burn rate (ie, how long it will take the company to burn through its cash and quick assets). To find the
company most likely to meet its daily cash expenditure, first use the quick ratio to find the quick assets; use the quick assets to determine the DIR.
In this scenario, since all three companies have the same daily cash expenditures of $50,000 and the same current liabilities of $1,500,000, the
company with the highest quick ratio, Company A, will have the largest amount of quick assets and the largest DIR.
Company A is most likely to meet is daily cash expenditures, since it has the highest DIR of 36.
(Choice B) This choice results from incorrectly using the cash ratio to determine the assets included in the DIR. Doing so excludes accounts
receivable, a quick asset, and understates the DIR.

harder to convert to cash than quick assets and results in an overstatement of the DIR.

explanation_en: Analysts use valuation models to estimate the intrinsic value of a stock to determine whether it is valued fairly. Common forms of valuation models include multiplier, present value, and asset based. With an asset-based valuation model, a firm's estimated equity value (ie, value to shareholders) is assumed to be equal to the current fair value of assets minus the fair value of liabilities. Analysts often start with the book values of line items on the balance sheet and make fair value adjustments to derive their market values. Since all inputs are based on current data, no long-term growth rate (g) is needed; g is used as an input for forecasting future cash flows (eg, dividends, free cash flows). (Choice A) When a multiplier model is justified (ie, justified P/E), it typically is derived from a present value model (eg, discounted free cash flow, dividend discount model), that includes g as an input. (Choice B) Present value models (eg, dividend discount model) typically require g for forecasting a company's future financial results (eg, dividends, free cash flows). Once forecasts are made, they are discounted to the present at an appropriate discount rate (eg, WACC) to derive an intrinsic value.

The sum of the discounted cash flows is the intrinsic value of the equity. A present value model uses cash flows to value equity. These cash flows may be dividends or free cash flows.
